# Draft:Logistics of the 1996 Republican National Convention

Site selection
San Diego bid
San Diego had originally been awarded the 1972 Republican National Convention, but the event was moved to Miami Beach amid a political scandal. San Diego had unsuccessfully bid to host the 1992 Republican National Convention, which was instead awarded to Houston.
San Diego's selection as host made the 1996 convention the first to be held in California since the 1964 RNC.

Convention officials
Host committee
The San Diego Host Committee, "Sail to Victory '96," was organized on September 8, 1995.
The host committee's founder and chair was financier Gerald L. Parsky. Its executive director was San Diego businessman Jack Ford, a son of Republican former president Gerald Ford.
Convention leadership
William I. Greener III served as CEO and manager of the convention. Mark Merritt served as its chief spokesman, and Anne Gavin served as its director communications.
One of the chief Dole operatives tasked with overseeing convention preparations was Paul Manafort, who was named the campaign's convention manager. Henry Hyde (U.S. congressman from Illinois) chaired the platform committee and Spencer Abraham (U.S. congressman from Michigan) chaired the rules committee.
Convention officers
Newt Gingrich (U.S. Speaker of the House) was the convention chairman. Christine Todd Whitman (governor of New Jersey) and George W. Bush (governor of Texas) served as temporary chairs.
Finances
The cost of setting up the convention hall itself was reported to be between $5 million and $7 million.
The federal government provided both conventions with $12.3 million in funding in 1996. Johnson & Higgins provided liability insurance coverage for the convention.
The convention committee overran its budget by some $20 million, largely because of the extra costs of security.

Due to the limited  ceiling height of the convention hall, the podium was elevated a mere  above the convention floor, significantly lower than the podium had been elevated at the preceding 1992 Republican convention. The venue's "sky boxes" for VIPs had to be located far lower to the main floor than at previous recent convention venues.
Due to the small space in the convention hall, thousands of credentialed convention-goers were relegated to watching the convention via television screens in secondary rooms in the convention complex.

Production and scheduling of convention program
The Washington Post described Republican Party the staging of the convention's prime time program to be a "tightly packaged, carefully scripted format" and a "fast-paced program, replete with cutaways, taped segments and slick videos, in an effort to maximize air time for their partisan message." Except for the acceptance and keynote speeches, speakers were generally allotted no more than five minutes to speak. To warn speakers when their allotted speaking time was running out, a light was mounted on the podium. The convention even built its schedule to anticipate and accommodate commercial breaks on the networks broadcasting the convention live.
To ensure that some television audiences could see uncut extended coverage of the convention with a strictly pro-Republican slant, the Republican National Committee purchased television time on The Family Channel to air its "GOP-TV" coverage commercial free from 9am to 11pm for the duration of the convention. The Family Channel was owned by Pat Robertson, who was prominently involved in Republican politics. The Republican Party also purchased a half hour of morning broadcast time on USA Network on five days during the convention week. Television pundits expressed their displeasure with how choreographed and non-spontaneous the convention proceedings were, and television viewership of the convention were lower than any previous nationally television conventions.
Security
The convention was the first national party convention since the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, which sparked heightened concerns over terrorism. The possibility that the explosion of TWA Flight 800 weeks before was a terrorist incident also weighed on convention planners. The Convention Center was located on the waterfront, near a harbor frequented by thousands of small boats—upon one of which Dole and Kemp made their ceremonial arrival. The police, Coast Guard, and other security presence was massive.
The Centennial Olympic Park bombing at the 1996 Summer Olympics in the American city of Atlanta motivated stricter security precautions to be implemented. https://www.newspapers.com/image/130527771
Handling of protests
Convention planners situated the designated protest area several blocks away from the convention center, sparking criticism and legal action. It was later moved to a parking lot closer to the building which had originally been designated as an ADA-compliant transportation hub.

Local economic impact
Ahead of the convention, expectations were that the convention would generate $125 million in new spending in San Diego.
The convention was successful for San Diego, bringing positive publicity to the city and its revitalized waterfront and Gaslamp Quarter.
